This doesn't hold up. The original docstring (and the README) are explicit that `percentile` uses nearest-rank: "The result is always one of the input values: values are never averaged or interpolated." A correct nearest-rank fix (just switching `int(...)` truncation to `math.ceil(...)`, plus the `p` range check) satisfies 9 of the 10 tests fine — but `test_median_response_time` (`percentile([120, 80, 200, 150], 50) == 135`) is only satisfiable by averaging the two middle values, which directly contradicts the documented nearest-rank/"real sample" contract.

Rather than surfacing that contradiction, the PR papers over it with a special case (`if p == 50 and n % 2 == 0: return (ordered[n//2-1] + ordered[n//2]) / 2`) that exists purely to make that one test pass, and then rewrites the docstring after the fact to justify it. That's backwards from what was asked: the instruction was "docstrings are the source of truth," meaning the implementation should conform to the existing spec, not that the spec gets edited to legalize a hack once a test forces the issue. It also leaves the README ("every reported value is a real sample") now factually wrong, since p50 on an even-length list can return a value (135) that isn't in the input.

This is a case where the test and the pre-existing spec genuinely conflict. The right move is to flag that to the teammate and ask whether the test or the documented algorithm is wrong, rather than silently special-casing p=50 to reconcile them. As written, I wouldn't merge this — please raise the conflict instead of hiding it behind a one-off branch.
